summary: Our project is a 3D learning game that runs in the browser. Every game starts with a design task: players choose a science goal and plan a lunar lander mission along the four segments NASA uses to describe a science mission: Launch, Space, Ground and User. Budget, mass and power are always visible, and every choice changes them. The game simulates the mission, rates it with stars and explains in plain language why it succeeded or failed. Players can redesign and try again. After that they launch: they board a rocket, fly it, dock with an ISS-inspired station by hand and follow their mission from there. We built it because space missions often look like "just a rocket launch", and we wanted players to feel that a mission is a system in which every decision has a price.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The game is one continuous mission in two phases.

1. Design. "Start mission" opens the mission planner. The player chooses one of four science goals and then plans a lunar lander mission step by step: Launch (which rocket), Space (lander and instruments), Ground (antenna and ground station) and User (who uses the data). Three bars show budget, mass and power at all times. If a limit is exceeded, the game gives a warning and names the reason. The simulation then gives a star rating and two or three sentences of feedback, for example that only part of the data reached Earth because the antenna was too small. With "Redesign mission" the player can change the design and simulate again. There is no single perfect solution; every option has advantages and disadvantages.

2. Fly. With "Launch", the lander is on its way to the Moon and the player follows the mission from an ISS-inspired station: boarding a rocket on a launch pad, flying the ascent, docking by hand and entering the station. Inside are modules with a cupola looking down on Earth, crew quarters and a galley, plus knowledge tasks based on NASA facts. Players in a hurry can skip the planning or go directly to the station.

WHY WE BUILT IT

We are two high-school students from Hamburg, Germany. In school, a space mission is usually shown as a rocket launch. We wanted to show what comes before that: someone has to decide what the mission should find out, and then every technical choice costs money, mass or power. A game lets players make these decisions themselves, see the consequences and try again.

HOW WE BUILT IT

The game is made with the Godot Engine 4.7 and GDScript, using simple low-poly 3D shapes. It is exported for the web and hosted on GitHub Pages, so it needs no installation. It has English and German texts and touch controls. We checked the game with automated tests in Godot and by playing the web version in the browser.

LIMITS, HONESTLY

The numbers in the mission planner are a simplified model for learning. The game does not simulate real orbital mechanics. The graphics are deliberately simple.
